873.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

874.content:
A module goes into a ship slot like any other. Where its effect can be seen, it is: a golden sail film unfolds above the
stern, a cloaked ship is wrapped in a violet shell with a running ring, the anchor braces against a black hole with rings of
light, the screen flashes a green hexagonal shell when it takes a hit, and the direction finder draws a dashed radio beam
from the nose to the source.

875.content: The data for projects comes from the instruments: “Radio telescope”, “The telescope and the sky”.

876.content: The other station module — “Zero-G Forge and star gear”.

877.content: Where the interstellar modules take you — “Interstellar space” (behind a spoiler).

879.content: The worlds’ inhabitants: trading, talking, tasks and reputation.

885.content:
Many worlds are home to **peoples** — each with its own look, crafts, settlements and attitude to a guest. All peoples
are in the reference.

886.content:
The people are at home in their world: the hail of their own weather (Jupiter’s mushballs, the Moon’s micrometeorites, the
Forge’s ember rain) does not hurt them, and one stuck in blocks steps out to a free spot by itself. They can still be hurt by a
blow, a fall and the visible events of a world — an eruption, a tornado, a storm’s lightning.

887.content:
Right-click an inhabitant to open a conversation: a greeting and topics you can ask about. The **elder** tells the most:
about the people, the world and the roads.

888.content:
Every settlement has a **chief** — the elder in its middle — and two or three **named masters**. They have their own names
(different in every settlement), a title in the window header and their own words; a crown rises above the chief's task mark,
a star above a master's. The chief gives a chain of tasks about the people's history with a reward found nowhere else; a master
gives a personal task. The people's page in the reference shows who they are.

889.content:
Every craft speaks in its own voice and gives **work beyond trade**: a cartographer sets your compass on a place for a compass
and a fee, a master mends the item in your hand, the elder tells the history and hints at the next step of a mystery, a herder
tells you about beasts — what to feed them and how to breed them. Click an inhabitant to hear their craft (a task shows as
"Q — task"); **Shift-click** opens trading at once. With talkative inhabitants the craft is the "Tell me about your work" answer.

890.content:
Every craft has its own trades by level — just like Earth’s villagers. The more you trade, the higher the level and the
more goods the inhabitant has.

891.content:
A golden “**!**” overhead means the inhabitant has a job for you. Take the task in conversation, complete it — bring
something their world lacks, defeat a creature, reach a place — and hand it in. The reward is items, experience and
**reputation** with the people. Each people has fifteen to twenty tasks across its crafts; a “**?**” overhead means a task
can be handed in.

892.content: The inhabitants give a map to their world’s dungeon: “Dungeons and world masters”.

893.content: In space the peoples keep stations with orders and trust: “Peoples’ stations, orders and trust”.

895.content: The dish, the radio map and the waterfall: how to tune the receiver to signals from the sky.

902.content:
Stars are joined with lines, seams are traced with the crosshair, vents are heard in rhythm — and radio is **tuned**. The
radio telescope shows no sky: at the top is a radio map, below it the **waterfall**: frequency left to right, time top to
bottom.

903.content:
sits on a mast of three , and around the receiver, at its level,
a 7 × 7 dish of . The receiver shows missing blocks as ghosts, and the last block placed
assembles the dish by itself. The dish looks where it was aimed and keeps tracking that point across the sky.

904.content:
The map is the real Galaxy: the disc and the bulge, bright sources at their real coordinates. What never rises over Earth
can be seen from the Moon or from your own station. Running machines closer than 24 blocks and thunderstorms cause
interference — put the dish away from your base. The dish does not go below 12° above the horizon: a lower source cannot be
recorded, and the beam panel tells you when it rises.

905.content:
The sky turns in step over Earth and over the Moon. “Wow!” comes once a sidereal day for 72 seconds, when Sagittarius
crosses the meridian — at the same moment everywhere: from Earth the source stands low in the south (about 23°), from the
Moon almost overhead, and in orbit it is always in view.

906.content: Every kind of signal has its own tuning control — the beam panel tells you which one to take, but not the solution.

907.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

908.content: Everyone around sees a find: the dish shoots a beam into the sky in the color of the source.

909.content:
Almost every fast radio burst comes once. One source — in Vulpecula — repeats: once in five days it sends a series of three
to six bursts in a night (the hint “when will the signal come” counts down to it). Point the dish at Vulpecula and
straighten the arcs with the dispersion wheel.

910.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

911.content:
Three radio telescopes on three roads — in the Solar System, in the Interrift and in the Depths — listen as one eye once
they are tied together by hydrogen clocks. Build a  from the blueprint
() and set it beside the receiver of an assembled telescope.

912.content:
Every four days comes the **night of Sagittarius** (a day and a half long); outside it the maser console says when the next
one begins. On the night press the maser and keep the crosshair on the drifting bright center for a minute — on every road it
moves in its own way. You get a .

913.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

914.content: From orbit the whole sky is visible: “Ships and space”.

915.content: Radio logs feed research projects: “Station Observatory”.

916.content: Where the navigation records lead — “Interstellar space” (behind a spoiler).

918.content: How to find a rift in the void of the End and tear open its seam.

923.content:
is the instrument of the dark road. It works only **in the End**, under the open sky and with
**four Eyes of Ender** in the sockets of its deck.

924.content:
The riftscope is a multiblock: a five-by-five deck, sockets in the middle of each side, a two-block column. The journal
shows the layout. An eye goes in by using it on the socket itself — like an End portal frame. When dismantled, the eyes
drop.

925.content:
| What to do      | How                       |
| --------------- | ------------------------- |
| Start observing | right-click the riftscope |

926.content:
| What to do  | How                                                                           |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Find a rift | follow the **void sparks**: they spiral toward the rift from all over the sky |

927.content:
| What to do            | How                                                                   |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tell that it is close | right at the rift the crosshair catches ripples and you hear knocking |

928.content:
| What to do    | How                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tear the seam | up close a seam shows — a broken line. Trace it with the crosshair **while holding the button**, segment by segment, from either end |

929.content:
| What to do  | How                                                            |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| If you slip | the last segment heals — take hold of any untouched part again |

930.content:

| ---------- | ----------- |
| Zoom       | mouse wheel |

931.content: A seam torn to the end opens into a rift, and the journal counts the find. All rifts are searched at once, in any order.

932.content:
Instead of shooting stars, little **cracks** flash in the End sky — catch them to get void shards. Shards pay for a call
(the hint key, H by default): for three shards it briefly shows the nearest unfound rift and drives all the sparks toward it,
and while it sounds an arrow at the edge of the screen shows which way to turn. A found rift brings four shards — enough for
the next call.

933.content: Beyond the rifts lie the four worlds of the dark road, reached by the shuttle. See “The roads”.

934.content: An opened rift changes the End itself: “Nether and End changes” and “Void Shoals”.

935.content: The worlds beyond the rifts have their own “Peoples and tasks”, “Dungeons and world masters” and “Gates”.

936.content: A ship of the dark road goes out into the Interrift: “Ships and space” and “Places of the Interrift” (behind spoilers).

937.content: How the road ends — “End of the Dark Road” (behind spoilers).

939.content: Who guards the places of the Ringwrights, how to fight it, what ring sparks are for and what the Ringwright Lens shows.

946.content:
**Watch rings** hang over the places the Ringwrights left behind. The first such place is the Monolith on the Moon; after
that, rings guard every niche with a tablet and the great places at the ends of the roads. Rings drop
, and sparks make the  — a lens that shows what the Ringwrights
left for those who look.

947.content:
A ring of light about two blocks across, held in four clasps of dark metal. It does not roam the world: each ring keeps
a post at its place and circles a few blocks away from it. Whoever it sees, it strikes with a beam, in a cycle:

948.content:
| Step    | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                 |
| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wind-up | 1 s      | the clasps tighten, the core flares, an aiming thread reaches for you — get out of its line |

949.content:
| Step | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                                                  |
| ---- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Beam | 1.5 s    | notched rims run from the ring to the target; the beam follows you with a lag — a step aside or a block in the way breaks it |

950.content:
| Step    | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                            |
| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cooling | 2 s      | the ring tilts and sinks, the clasps open — **it takes half again as much damage**, time for the sword |

951.content:
**The danger sign.** A ring that has taken aim at you shows even when it is behind your back: a ring of light tightens on
the floor around your feet (under the beam it burns and ripples outward), and a line rises above the hotbar — “A watch ring
takes aim at you — step out of its beam”. The line shows over an open window too, even while you read a tablet. The sign
looks the same at every “Mod graphics” level.

952.content:
24 health. It never follows a target farther than 26 blocks from its post; walled in by blocks, it drifts back to the
post straight through them.

953.content:
It does not see players in Creative or spectators. With friends, each ring strikes whoever it sees itself and burns
anyone who steps into the beam.

954.content:
The beam burns but does not push: it will not knock you off a stair or a narrow bridge. Armor soaks it like an
ordinary hit.

955.content: It does not appear on Peaceful or with `spawn_mobs false`.

956.content:
It does not stand on a path: over the steps of a stair (the spiral steps in the well of the Swarm Archive) or in a
passage one block wide a ring neither appears nor circles — you walk to the niche, not through it.

957.content:
**How many**: no more than three at one place and four near one player. A place raises a new ring at most once
every 10 seconds and rests a minute or two after a ring dies — no farming sparks faster than about one a minute.

958.content: A ring drops a  70% of the time.

959.content: The ring’s light, curled up into a spark. It goes into:

960.content: the  — four sparks; on an anvil a spark gives the Lens back a quarter of its charge;

961.content:
the tier II and III modules of the far roads — one spark per recipe: interstellar drives
(, ), spindle keels
(, ) and crucible jackets
(, );

962.content: the  — two sparks in its forge recipe;

963.content:
Ringwright decor: the  (a ring of light on a stand, light 14) and
 (glowing seams).

964.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

965.content: **How to wear it**: in either hand, or over the eye — in a slot mod: the face slot of Trinkets, the head slot of Curios (NeoForge).

966.content:
**Charge** — 1200 seconds of showing. It drains second by second only while the Lens has something to show: a place
of the Ringwrights or a hidden block within 48 blocks. It never breaks at zero — it goes dark; relight it with a ring
spark on an anvil.

967.content:
**What you see**: at an open niche — the Ringwrights’ script right on the walls (signs you already understand in
turquoise, the rest in violet), a ring print with nine notches on the floor before the niche (up to nine blocks across; smaller in a cramped room, but never under three) and a palm
print by the opening; from afar — a trail of huge footprints toward the nearest niche, but only eight steps ahead: the
rest is yours to find. The layer washes out from you in a wave over a second and a half.

968.content:
**For you alone**: what the Lens shows is seen only by the one looking through it — a friend beside you without a Lens
sees nothing.

969.content: A sealed niche is smooth stone: the Lens does not give it away and spends no charge near it; open the place first.

970.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

971.content: Rings strike one at a time, in turn: keep an eye on the one drawing its aiming thread and hit the one that is cooling.

972.content: A wall or pillar between you and a ring breaks its beam — there is almost always cover near a niche.

973.content: The Lens in your off hand keeps the main hand free for the sword; over the eye it keeps both free.

974.content: The gate rings are their work too: “Gates”.

975.content: The great places at the ends of the roads: “End of the Dark Road” and “End of the Fire Road” (behind spoilers).

976.content: Records that can be read only through the Lens: knots (“The Underweave”) and hallmarks (“The Underdeep”).

978.content: Fuel, the launch pad, assembling a rocket and flying to a world you have found.

984.content:
A world found through the telescope can be visited. Rockets come in four tiers: **lunar, interplanetary, heavy and deep
space** — each flies further than the one before.

985.content:
— fuel: open the plant, put in coal and empty canisters (two pieces of coal fill a canister);
hoppers work with it as with a chest.

986.content:
— charge: under the open sky by day it charges flat batteries, half a minute each.
Every flight drains one battery.

987.content: — the launch pad; the rocket is assembled on it and does not take it along at launch.

988.content: A battery block charges batteries from the grid of the base machines too, see “Machines and energy”.

989.content:
Build the rocket on the pad from the bottom up — the journal shows the layout; it assembles itself once the last block
is in place (on the lunar one, the nose cone above the cabin). The layout is tied to the compass, not to the cabin: the interplanetary rocket's boosters go on the west and east sides, the fins on the north and south, and once assembled its cabin turns to face north or south. A gauge on the front of the tank shows the fuel, the lights
on the fins and the cabin windows show the charge. The tiers are told apart from afar by their silhouette: the lunar
rocket is stout, on four red fins; the interplanetary one is tall, with two boosters, a black heat-shield band and an
escape tower above the capsule; the heavy one is a thick tower on a white "skirt" of four boosters, with a checkered
section and a blunt red nose; the deep space one is a ship on five engines with spherical tanks, a habitat ring (it
spins while there is charge) and an antenna dish on top. On the heavy and deep space rockets the gauge shows helium,
and the coil rings above the nozzles glow orange.

990.content:
Sit in the cabin and open the **star map**: you can only fly to a world found through the telescope, and only with open
sky above the rocket.

991.content:
The rocket lands where it stood before in that world, and in a new world it looks for a flat free spot. It breaks
nothing and never lands amid lava: there is always solid ground to step out onto, and it keeps clear of the lava sea of Venus.

992.content:
**Pack for the way back before you go.** For the chosen world the star map says what it takes to lift off from there:
fuel for the way back, a charged battery (the flight drains it, and the lunar rocket has only one), a return stage (a new world
has no launch pad, and none can be built under a landed rocket) — and landing legs: without them only the cabin comes down,
with an empty tank. Home the rocket flies the same way, back to its pad. A rocket on the pad can also be filled through pipes — by the fueling and charging
gantries.

993.content:
A rocket has module sockets on its hull: two on the lunar rocket, three on the interplanetary, four on the heavy and six
on the deep-space rocket. Fit a module by using it on a hull socket (sneak with an empty hand to take it off), or put it
into the module slots of the cabin window. Every module shows on the rocket itself and is easy to tell from afar:

994.content:
— two legs splayed sideways with feet, under a yellow-and-black striped housing:
the whole rocket lands, not just the cabin.

995.content: — a little rocket on a black nozzle bell: take off from bare ground, no launch pad.

996.content: — a crate of chest planks under an iron lid: nine slots of cargo.

997.content: — a hump with a porthole that glows warm: room for a second passenger.

998.content: — a barrel with a red band and fuel glowing in its sight glass: half as much fuel again.

999.content: — a copper cabinet with two terminals and red charge bars: two more battery slots.

1000.content: — two blue wings: parked under the open sky, the rocket slowly charges itself.

1001.content: — a fan over a blue glow of air: you can breathe in the cabin and next to the landed rocket.

1002.content: — a pair of white boosters that burn in flight too: a flight costs a fifth less.

1003.content:
— a white dish with a blinking lens: after landing it tells you which way the nearest
settlement is.

1004.content:
The dark and fire roads have no rockets: the **shuttle** goes to the worlds beyond the rifts, the **bell** to the bottom
of the vents. Where the craft may go is decided by modules: the module for the next world is made from the spoils of the
previous one.
A module goes on the craft itself: click a socket on the hull with it in hand (sneak-click with an empty hand to take it
off). Every departure from the End or the Nether costs a spool of thread or an ember-tempered chain and fuel by the
world's distance, while the way back along the thread or chain is free, back to its dock or winch. A trip from world to world adds
up both distances and can exceed the tank (from the Hive to the Eye it is 12 against a tank of 10): then go home first.
The craft's console says "Ready to go" only when its supplies reach at least one found world; otherwise it says what is
missing: "Not enough liquid pearl: the nearest world takes 3".

1005.content: Before the first launch — “Oxygen, spacesuit and climate”: you cannot breathe in the mod’s worlds.

1006.content: “Machines and energy” — where the fuel and the charge come from.

1007.content: On arrival you will find “Peoples and tasks”, “Dungeons and world masters” and “Gates”.

1008.content: The shuttle and the bell start with their own instruments: the “Riftscope” and the “Magmascope”.

1009.content: Later a ship of your own replaces the rocket: “Ships and space”.

1011.content: The shipyard, ship forms and classes, modules, flight over a world and going out into space.

1016.content: In the cockpit: labels, zoom, picking a target

1024.content:
A ship is late-game transport. It flies over a world like a plane, climbs above the sky — and finds itself in the space
of its road, where worlds are spheres in the sky.

1025.content:
A ship is welded at the **shipyard** from parts — which ones, the form page shows. The form sets the
role (scout, freighter, warship…), the hull, hold, tank and the number of module slots. The ship’s **class** multiplies
speed, hull, hold, jump and scanner.

1026.content:
You build the shipyard yourself: the shipyard console at the middle of a long side of a 9 × 5 slipway, two crane towers of
four sections at opposite corners (the scheme and its Show in the world button are on the Shipyard page of the star journal);
clicking the console shows what is missing. The shipyard knows the scout of your road once you beat the road's first master
(Terminator Warden, Mother of the Comb, Giant's Remnant) and the hauler after the last one; other forms come from blueprints
in space caches and stations.

1027.content:
Modules go into slots: thrust, hull, hold, scanner and others, each with tiers I–III. A tier is made from the metals of
its road.

1028.content:
Over a world the ship flies like a plane: cruise, boost, turns, climb. Above the sky begins the space of the road: belts,
comets, the peoples’ stations and anomalies. A ship can be picked up into the hold by a beam, towed, and you can transfer
to another one.

1029.content:
Someone else’s ship (two players) can be refueled and mended by anyone, but only its owner takes the helm: a guest comes
aboard through the stern hatch while the owner is home, and rides as a passenger in a two-seater once the owner is in the
cockpit. Clicking such a ship says exactly that — whose it is and what it takes. Only the owner opens the ship console
(modules and hold) — from outside and from the passenger seat alike.

1030.content:
While you are aboard — as the pilot or a passenger — you are behind the hull: claws, projectiles and beams of creatures hit
the hull instead of you, at half strength. The hull does not last forever: a wrecked ship no longer shelters you. Heat, cold
and radiation are not stopped this way — those are for the suit and modules.

1031.content:
From space a ship enters a world's sky where it touches the globe — come back to Earth from the wrong side and you can land twenty
thousand blocks from your base. For free, the globe keeps the **Takeoff pad** — where the ship last left that world for space:
fly within 1500 blocks of the mark and the ship enters the sky right above it.

1032.content:
The  is help that costs resources: put it under the open sky by your base in a world you enter
from space (Earth, planets, moons, small worlds), and the ship enters the sky right above it from wherever it reaches the globe.
Only you and your team (`/team`) see it: from the ground, a beam into the sky; from space, a glint on the globe and the line
"Entering above beacon: name". By the globe the mouse wheel picks another beacon or none; the autopilot aimed at a world with a
beacon stops right above it. Up to four lit beacons per player in a world; name it on an anvil or with a name tag. Rockets do
not use it: they already land on your previous pad.

1033.content:
The beacon also works in the eight worlds beyond the End's rifts and at the bottom of Nether vents. A void or depth ship that
flies into a world's hole comes out in the sky above the chosen beacon (the mouse wheel by the hole, as by a globe), and the
Takeoff Pad mark remembers where it left through the hole. The Rift Shuttle and the Diving Bell land beside the beacon — a few
steps from the beam, not on your previous pad: they have no wheel to pick, so they take the first beacon of whoever is aboard.

1034.content:
In the Nether itself the beacon needs open space above it instead of the sky. A depth ship coming up from the Depths through
the vault surfaces in the Nether right beside your beacon, wherever it rose; without a beacon it surfaces where it dove into
the lava, if it comes up within 1500 blocks of that spot (the Takeoff Pad mark is shown on the vault). It always surfaces in
a free space big enough for the whole ship, never inside the rock; with no room anywhere near, it stays in the Depths. The
Diving Bell returning to the Nether lands on the pad it took off from.

1035.content:
**Labels in the sky.** Labels that would overlap fold into one, the most important, with “+N”: from the outskirts the
Sun shows as “Sun +19”, not two dozen names. A label hidden behind a nearby body (a ship, a boulder, a comet nucleus,
a station, a creature) fades. The **F10** key cycles labels: all → target and important → hidden. Danger signs are
always visible.

1036.content:
**Zoom.** Hold “pick block” (the mouse wheel) or your own “zoom” key in the controls: the field of view narrows like a
spyglass, and labels spread apart and grow larger. The wheel sets the power (×3, ×6, ×12), the right button the filter
(all, bodies, stations, anomalies), the left button picks a target. The card of the aimed target says what it is, how
far, and whether you can jump there — and if not, why: the ship is on a tether, not enough fuel (how much is needed and
how much is in the tank), closer than 1,500 blocks — fly there under your own power. The jump charges toward the picked
target, and the autopilot leads to it.

1037.content:
**Instruments do not overlap.** Side panels (scanner, radio, anomaly steps, comet nucleus, combat) stand in columns; when
space is tight the less important one folds into a line; key hints form a column in the lower left corner.

1038.content: **Ship friends** in the console (Shift + right-click the ship) scroll with the wheel; type a name and the list filters.

1039.content:
The **F8** key (Ship: System Map in the controls) opens the **System Map**, a top-down hologram of the whole current cosmos:
bodies, orbits, asteroid belts and fields, known stations and your team. It works in the cockpit, aboard and on foot in any
cosmos; on a far road the same key opens that road's own map, and buttons lead to the Interstellar, Pattern and Section maps
if you have them.

1040.content:
**A fisheye scale**: true to size near the middle and squeezed toward the edge, so Mercury and the Kuiper belt fit in one view.
The wheel zooms toward the point under the cursor, drag to move. The rings are distances: from the Sun, from the ship (To the
ship keeps the middle on your ship) or, on foot, from you (To me); Whole system shows the whole cosmos again.

1041.content:
**Only your own finds**: the map shows only what your ship's scanner has found: stations, expedition caches, rich rocks,
fields, anomalies you noticed. Things that stay put are remembered after you leave the game; moving ones (the comet,
creatures) read "Seen N min ago" and fade after five minutes. Close marks of one kind merge into a counted heap ("Expedition
cache ×9"): click it and the map zooms in until the heap opens.

1042.content:
**Distance and time**: under the cursor, how many blocks it is from the ship (on foot, from you) and how long it takes at cruise
and at your current speed; for the target the same, plus whether you can land there and whether you can jump.

1043.content:
**Target**: click a body or mark, **Set as target**, and the **Autopilot to the target** button (from the pilot seat) flies the
ship there. The autopilot now also flies to fields, caches, rich rocks and anomalies, stopping forty blocks from their edge.

1044.content:
The scanner's **Rich rock** marks do not lie: every marked rock of a belt holds an ore heart of the ore the mark names, in its
middle, right where the mark points.

1045.content:
Jumps to a comet and to the Visitor are led: the marker stands where the target will be at the end of the jump. At a
comet you exit beyond the edge of the danger zone, at the Visitor a hundred blocks behind it, in its wake, matching its
speed.

1046.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1047.content:
The Visitor’s disc is made of large boulders. Bring the ship over a boulder from above and match speed, without pressing
forward or up — the landing legs settle on the stone, and the ship rides along with the Visitor even with nobody aboard.
Stepping out, you stand on the boulder and can walk on it; step off the edge or jump, and the Visitor slips away from
under your feet. You cannot land on a comet: its nucleus tumbles.

1048.content:
After a scan, the comet heart shows as a marker through the ice. It is deep inside a large clump and cannot be taken by
hand: dig with the **mining beam** (left Alt) through the crust and ice. The mining beam is a ship module: it is made at a
crafting table from titanium, a lens, a coil and a battery (or traded from the Fear Drillers) and fitted into a slot of
the ship’s console.

1049.content: The anomaly steps tell you what to do with your hands, and show an instrument at the moment of the attempt.

1050.content:
**Slingshot** — pass the hole closer than 260 blocks (but not closer than 40) on boost and turn: the arc must be 50°
or more. In the sky there are rings for the 600 and 260 zones; the instrument counts the arc (“18° more”) and tells you
if you are too far or too slow. Leave the 600 zone and the maneuver counts.

1051.content:
**Ride the jet** — during an outburst enter the ring at the base of the column (the “stream entry” marker), not the red
one, and hold on in the sheath for five seconds. Where the nose points, there you are thrown — the instrument says
toward what.

1052.content:
A ship can be dismantled or refitted only on the shipyard’s slipway: put it on the slipway and hold the “Dismantle”
button in the shipyard screen for a second and a half.

1065.content:
An ore sample, a creature part, a gas or the light of a star give a **spectrum**. Match its lines with the references — the
real lines of substances — and you learn the substance, and with it the recipes made from it.

1070.content:
The lines are real — from the reference tables: hydrogen’s Balmer series, the sodium D lines, calcium H and K, oxygen
bands. Where the game takes liberties, the reference text says so. If a sample holds two unknown substances, you need a
simpler sample.

1071.content: On a telescope, the spectrograph shows which bodies have air and life.

need not be solved again: put it in the laboratory and press **Open the sample**, one spark of the laboratory's charge per sample.
With Shift the button reads **Open them all**: the rest in the holder and the same samples from your inventory. The sample's
tooltip says what it is and what may be inside, or that it still has to be identified. JEI and REI show it as its own page,
Opening Samples.

1084.content:
The zero-g forge is a module of your own station (): a glass sphere between four magnetic
pillars with the chamber heart () in the middle. Without weight the melt neither settles
nor separates, so here you forge what no planet can cast: star gear made from the materials of the Solar System.

1085.content: Press the forge console — a window opens with the recipe book on the left.

1086.content:
Press a recipe: the materials from your inventory lay themselves into the four cells (the rest goes back). Whatever is
missing, the window names in a line.

1087.content:
The “Forge” button starts the chamber. Drops of metal in the recipe’s colors rise in the sphere, circle, merge into
the piece, arcs jump between the pillars — and a flash at the end.

1088.content: The finished piece waits in the output cell. Forging runs on world time: you can leave and come back.

1089.content:
There is one forge per station, and it forges one piece at a time. The forge belongs to the station, like its hold: the
window opens only for the station's owner, and a guest is told “This is not your station”.

people’s **trust**. The mouse wheel flips through the cards.

how many you already carry. Orders are taken, dropped and handed in at the board.

1142.content:
A late parcel or weekly order costs −10 trust, a failed convoy −6. You see a loss at once: a line
“Trust · people: −N — why” in the uplink and in chat.

1143.content:
Take the race and fly to the station: a track of twelve rings of light rises around it. The clock starts at the first
ring. The next ring shines brighter than the rest and points the way on with a beam. Missing a ring does not end the race
but adds 5 seconds. Your instruments show the timer, the ring number and how far behind the station record you are. The
record (name and time) is shown on the race card at the board. A freighter makes it on the limit, a scout with time to spare.

1144.content:
At Interrift stations the rings are woven of threads, at Depths stations they are made of magma. The first race you hand
in gives the : a pennant of light flies behind your ship, a golden one for a record holder.

1145.content:
Take a convoy and fly your ship to the meeting point (a mark in the sky, 350 blocks from the station): the station’s cargo
drone comes out to meet you. The drone only moves while you are within 160 blocks and heads for a buoy 3,000–3,600 blocks
away. At one third and two thirds of the way drifters attack it, three ships first, then four. The raiders go for the cargo and
ignore your ship until you shoot at them, but every second ship of a wave is a hunter that comes straight for you. Choose whom
to shoot first: while you chase the hunter, the others wreck the drone (its hull is 120; a wave nobody drives off destroys it in
a little over a minute). Slow down as you close in: at full speed it is easy to miss the ships circling the drone. On a class B
Hornet with a single Pulse Cannon II the convoy is risky — you reach the buoy with about half your hull; on a class A ship
with Cannon III and a shield it is easy. Fall behind for more than a minute and the drone turns home, and the convoy fails. At the buoy the drone jumps, and
you can hand the order in at the board. If you own a station, its cargo drones on their runs also go under the people’s
guard. You can only escort one convoy at a time.

1154.content: The drifters’ den has no board: there is no dealing with drifters, they are only enemies.

1155.content:
**Station team.** The owner of a player station can let friends use it, with everything open to them as to the owner: modules
and tiers, the hangar, the hold, workshops, the observatory, the Zero-G Forge, the bunk and the crew; the station refinery fuels
their ships. Crouch and use an empty hand on a socket of your station to open the **Station team** window: on the left the owner
and the team (nearby, online, offline), on the right the online players you can add (type a name to search). A team holds up to
eight players and only the owner edits it; whoever is removed has the station windows closed. The same works with the mod's
command `station trust add|remove|list <player>` while standing on the station; no operator rights are needed for your own.

1156.content:
Observatory forecasts go to the whole team online, and a finished project reaches every team member. Fuel from the refinery
tanks and the free fuel at the dock go only to the owner and the team: a stranger's ship cannot drain the station.

1157.content:
**Station name.** The owner can rename the station: the pencil after the name in the title of the Station team window (Enter
saves, Esc cancels, an empty name brings back the orbit name such as "Earth-I"), or the command `station name <name>`,
`station name reset`. A name is up to 32 characters and everyone sees it: on the scanner, the System Map, the HUD and in messages.

1180.content:

closed. A finished constellation flares up, its stars lighting one after another; the journal records it, and new stages
open after it.

1181.content:
When you are stuck — staring at a constellation without new lines for a long time or making two mistakes in a row — the
telescope offers a hint: a plate with a key and a price. A hint reveals **one** line, and you draw it yourself. You pay
in stardust; stardust comes from shooting stars caught in the crosshair and from discoveries in the sky. In creative
mode hints are free.

1182.content:
The Moon, the planets and distant bodies are not visible to every telescope: the refractor, reflector, astrograph and
graviscope each see further. The journal records a body you have found, and then you can fly to it. Where to look for
each body is hinted by the journal itself — the wiki does not give these answers away.

1183.content:
The sky is visible through glass, while mountains, houses and mobs block it — just like the real one. With a shader
pack the telescope sky is drawn over the frame and still works.

1271.content:
Once a rift is open in the End, pale **void currents** in the color of that rift rise from the void at the edges of the outer
islands on its side of the sky. This is where you dive: jump with a safety line, let the currents carry you, and catch the finds
drifting in them. While the End sleeps (stage 0, see “Nether and End changes”) or the changes
are switched off, there are no currents and no finds; the main island is left alone — currents rise only by the outer islands.

1272.content:
A current stands **at an island edge**: a column from the bottom of the world up to the rim, two blocks above the ground.
Its axis slowly moves in a circle.

1273.content:
Inside a current you are lifted — faster at the axis, slower at the edge; toward the top the lift fades and you hover at the
rim while the current carries you to it. Over the ground it lets go — you step onto the island.

1274.content: **Between currents you fall.** Below 22 blocks above the bottom, the void pulls down harder than normal gravity.

1275.content: With an elytra, a current is an updraft. During Void Pull the currents are a third stronger.

1276.content: The deeper the dive, the richer the finds.

1360.content:
The mod ships as **six files**: one per Minecraft version and loader. The game version and the loader are in the
file name:

1364.content:
All of them have the same content; install the one for your game version and loader. There is no single jar for Fabric
and NeoForge or for different game versions; on 1.20.1 the one `…-forge-…` file runs on both Forge 47 and NeoForge 47.1.
A few things look or work a little differently on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1: vanilla clouds are sparser
(that is how these versions draw them), stars in open space are a little smaller, and on NeoForge 1.21.1 and Forge 1.20.1 artifacts go only into
Curios slots. These versions have no copper nugget, so there the crusher does not break a Copper Sheet, Wiring or a Copper Coil
down into nuggets, and the Smoker Crab does not drop them. A world does not move between game versions.

1365.content:
Both files carry the mod description for their loader, so launchers and sites show the name, version and loader
by themselves. In the NeoForge mod list a second line marked “(resources)” sits next to the mod — these are its own
resources, nested in the same jar: nothing else needs installing.

1366.content: Install Fabric Loader for the right Minecraft version.

1367.content:
Put the mod’s Fabric file, **Fabric API** and **GeckoLib** for Fabric (the mod’s models and animations) into the
`mods` folder — all three for the same Minecraft version. On 1.21.1 that is **GeckoLib 4** (4.9.3 or newer), on 1.20.1 GeckoLib 4 (4.8.4 or newer),
on 26.3 — GeckoLib 5.

1368.content: Launch the game with the Fabric profile. Java must be the version listed in the table.

1369.content: Mod settings — via **Mod Menu** (if installed) or the gear in the Star Journal.

1370.content:
Install NeoForge for your Minecraft version: 21.1 for 1.21.1, or 26.3 — NeoForge is still
in beta for 26.3.

1371.content:
Put the mod’s NeoForge file and **GeckoLib** for NeoForge into the `mods` folder (GeckoLib 4 on 1.21.1, GeckoLib 5
on 26.3). Nothing else is required.

1372.content: Launch the game with the NeoForge profile.

1373.content:
Mod settings — the Config button in the mod list or the gear in the journal. Machine energy is NeoForge’s shared energy
(FE), fluids and items use NeoForge transfer: cables, pipes and tanks of other mods connect to the machines, just as on

1374.content: Install Forge 47 or NeoForge 47.1 for Minecraft 1.20.1. You need Java 17.

1375.content: Put the `…-forge-1.20.1-<version>.jar` file and **GeckoLib** for Forge (4.8.4 or newer) into the `mods` folder. Nothing else is required.

1376.content: Launch the game with the Forge or NeoForge profile.

1377.content: Machine energy on Forge is shared Forge energy (FE), fluids and items use Forge transfer, as on NeoForge above.

1384.content:
The mod goes **both on the server and on every player’s client**: rules and state live on the server, the client draws.
The server and the players use the same file — the same loader and the same Minecraft version: a Fabric client cannot
join a NeoForge server, a 1.21.1 client cannot join a 26.3 or 1.20.1 server, and vice versa. More —
“Playing on a server”; the same page has a short part for administrators:
the mod’s command and how the mod is checked on a dedicated server.

1385.content:
**`class file version 69.0 … up to 65.0`.** The error `java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: … has been compiled by a more
recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file
versions up to 65.0` means the game was started with an old Java: 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21. Minecraft 26.3 needs
**Java 25**, and it is the game itself that fails, before any mod loads (Minecraft 1.21.1 runs on Java 21, 1.20.1 on Java 17). Install Java 25 (for example from
Adoptium) and select it in your launcher’s installation settings; the official launcher and most
others pick the right Java on their own. On a server — see “The server won’t start”.

1386.content:
**Fabric: an “Incompatible mods found!” window** with the line `requires version … or later of fabric-api, which is missing`
(or `… of geckolib …`) — Fabric API or GeckoLib is not in the `mods` folder. The loader tells you what to install:
`Install geckolib, version 5.5.7 or later`.

1387.content:
**NeoForge: `requires geckolib 5.5.7 or above. Currently, geckolib is not installed`** — GeckoLib for NeoForge is not
in the `mods` folder.

1683.content: The mod’s three roads — the sky, the dark and the fire — briefly and without spoilers.

1688.content:
The mod has three roads. Each starts with its own instrument, leads through its own worlds and needs its own transport.
You can take any of them in any order, but the journal leads along the sky road first.

1689.content:
It starts with a telescope on Earth. Telescopes grow — refractor, reflector, astrograph, graviscope — and each sees
further: first the constellations and the Moon, then the planets. A world you have found can be visited by rocket: the
lunar, interplanetary, heavy and deep-space rockets fly further and further. Beyond that the road leads to your own
ships and open space.

1690.content:
The road’s worlds are the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, the giant planets and their small worlds. In detail — in the
world reference.

1691.content:
It starts in the End. The riftscope looks not at the stars but into the void: rifts hide in it, and you have to find
them and tear them open along the seam. Beyond the rifts lie four worlds, reached by the **shuttle**. See
“Riftscope”. How it ends — behind a spoiler.

1692.content:
It starts in the Nether. The magmascope looks down into a bowl of lava: vents are found by ear and opened with strikes
in time with their pulse. At the bottom of the vents lie worlds of fire, reached by the **bell**. See
“Magmascope”. How it ends — behind a spoiler.

1693.content: Every world has a **master** — a boss at the heart of that world’s dungeon. While it lives, the world’s gate sleeps.

1694.content:
**Gates** — nine-by-nine rings on all the worlds at once. Awakened gates link the worlds, bypassing transport.
See “Gates”.

1695.content:
**Peoples** live on many worlds: you trade with them, talk to them and take their tasks. See
“Peoples and tasks”.

1698.content: The mod on a dedicated server: installation, playing together and server load.

1701.content: The mod is made for playing with friends: everything works on a dedicated server with several players.

1702.content:
**Installed on the server and on every player** — the same versions of the mod and its dependencies, the same
Minecraft version (26.3, 1.21.1 or 1.20.1) and the same loader, Fabric, NeoForge or Forge (see “Installation”).
Servers on 1.20.1 run on Java 17, servers on 1.21.1 on Java 21, servers on 26.3 on Java 25.

1703.content:
**Everyone has their own path**: the journal, found worlds, the spacesuit, tasks and the trust of the peoples are
per player. Worlds, buildings and gates are shared.

1704.content: **Together** you can fly in one rocket, crew a ship, transfer to a friend’s ship and tow a downed ship.

1705.content:
**Knowledge by copy**: to catch up with a friend who has gone ahead, use a Journal Copy: it carries
stages, finds, the Atlas of Life and other knowledge, while deeds (landings, victories, rewards) stay each player's own.

1706.content:
**Your station for a team**: the owner lets friends onto their own station with the Station team window or the `station trust`
command, see Your own station: team and name.

1707.content:
**Sleep and events**: while one of a world's events is on (the blood moon and the rest), nobody can sleep there: the bed names
the event but still sets the spawn point, and an event wakes those asleep. Other worlds sleep as usual.

1708.content:
**Your seat waits for you**: if you leave the game aboard a ship you were not flying alone, the seat stays yours — when
you come back you are aboard again, in your own seat, wherever the ship has got to by then. A crew also survives a server
restart: the ship is in place and everyone is seated. Alone aboard, the ship still leaves the world with you and returns
with you, as before. The same holds in a rocket, the End shuttle and the Nether bell with a passenger seat: leave during
lift-off and you come back into your seat wherever the craft is flying; if it has landed without you, you step out
beside it, next to the others. If the craft is gone (the ship was destroyed while you were away), you are brought to
safety — to the ground nearby or to your respawn point — and if your seat has been taken, the ship lets you aboard, on
the deck. A line on the screen tells you so.

1709.content:
**Light on the server**: the mod does not walk every block and entity every tick, does heavy work less often and on
events, and sends packets only on change. This is checked by measuring on a server with players.

1710.content:
**Fast flight does not stall the server**: chunks along a ship’s course are prepared in advance, and where they are
still being generated the server does not wait for them mid-tick. Light under growing islands and boss beams are sent
sparingly — in one packet and as keyframes.

1711.content:
The client only draws and sends intentions — the server decides: whether a world is found, a stage is counted, a
rocket has arrived.

1712.content:
**Checked by two players.** Before release the whole mod is walked through by two players on a real dedicated server,
on Fabric and on NeoForge: 63 scenes, from joining and machine windows to ships, small worlds and their events, the far roads and the
finale, with players leaving mid-flight, dropped connections and a server restart. After a drop and after the restart
everything a player has is compared: world and place, progress, spacesuit, tasks, inventory, the ship under them.

1713.content:
**A stop in the middle of the Free Haven fight.** The raiders' lair on Deimos keeps in the world data how many of its
ships and turrets are still standing and how much damage each player has dealt to them. After a server restart the
surviving defenders come out again, and the shares of those who fought before the stop are intact. The journal key for
sacking the haven also waits for a player who fought its defenders but was offline when it fell: they get it a few
seconds after joining. The share items themselves lie by the haven for twelve minutes
(a downed raider's wreck — three), and a server restart does not wipe them: the spoils are kept in the world data, each
share waits for its own player and nobody else can take it — fly by in a ship and it goes into the hold.

1714.content:
**Nether and End changes.** The Nether and the End change in stages, shared by the whole server, as players open rifts, vents
and the roads beyond them (Nether and End changes). A server owner can switch the changes off with
the game rule Nether and End changes (`/gamerule`, under the mod id, `nether_end_changes`) or with
`"nether_end_changes": false` in `config/<mod id>-server.json`: stages still build up, but nothing is shown.

1715.content:
**The mod has one command**, named the same as the mod id; it needs operator rights. To run it for a player, use
`execute as <player> run …`.

1716.content:
| Command                | What it does                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `progress grant <key>` | counts one progress key: to restore something lost. `progress complete` and `progress reset` set the whole journal path at once |

1717.content:
| Command                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `structure restore <id> [radius] [force]` | puts a mod structure into the world of whoever gave the command, where it belongs — for old worlds whose chunks were generated without it (up to 0.15.2 the Ring at the Edge and other one-per-world structures were missing in some worlds, and `/locate` hung on them). It searches from the caller outwards (3072 blocks by default), records the structure so `/locate` finds it, and does not clear what already stands there; `force` places it again |

1718.content:
| Command                | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `rocket land [player]` | lands a craft (rocket, shuttle, bell) stuck in flight: the one the player sits in (without a player — the caller), or, if they are not aboard one, the nearest craft taking off, on its way or waiting over a world. A craft that has not left yet is moved to the world it is flying to, onto its usual landing site; the flight ends for those aboard, and the craft lands and turns back into blocks. It should not get stuck anyway: over the new world a craft waits for its passengers no longer than 15 seconds, and the player's space scene ends by itself when they are not aboard |

1719.content:

1726.content:
**`class file version 69.0 … up to 65.0`.** If the server dies at once and the console shows
`java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: … has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file
version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0` (on Fabric the line above
it is `An exception occurred when launching the server!`), the server was started with Java 21, and Minecraft 26.3 needs
**Java 25**: 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21 (a 1.21.1 server is fine on Java 21 — check that the server and the mod file
are for the same Minecraft version). The mod has nothing to do with it — a server without mods fails the same way.
Install Java 25 and point the server at it: on a host — in the panel (Java version or an image with Java 25), on your own
machine — with the full path to `java` in the start command (for NeoForge — in `run.sh` or `run.bat`). `java -version`
shows which Java is being started.

1744.content:
Low graphics lighten the decoration, not what you play by: danger signs are visible at every level. The game’s
“Particles” setting reduces the mod’s particles too.

1745.content:
**Effects with shader packs** is a switch in the mod settings. With a shader pack (Iris, Oculus) the mod's post-effects turn
off by themselves; switch it on and they run with the pack too, at your own risk: the pack may spoil them (a black screen or
streaks: switch it off again). Tested with Complementary and Bliss.

1746.content:
The mod's screens (the journal, machine consoles, the storage terminal and others) are drawn in finer detail than the game's
own, and their small text is smaller than the game's letters. If they look too small at the GUI Scale that suits the game's
screens, the mod settings have a choice on the right of the Mod graphics line:

1747.content: **Match game** (the default) — the mod's screens follow GUI Scale, like the game's own;

1748.content: **Larger** — halfway to the largest, whatever GUI Scale is set to;

1749.content: **Largest** — always the largest that fits the game window, as with “GUI Scale: Auto”.

1750.content:
On a 1920×1080 screen Larger and Largest are the same, and at 1366×768 and smaller the mod's screens are the largest anyway.
The choice takes effect at once, even on an open screen; the game's screens and the mod's HUD do not change.

1751.content:
The whole screen grows, your inventory included: in machine consoles, the storage terminal and ship windows its slots,
items and stack counts on a 1920×1080 screen at GUI Scale 2–3 are as large as in the game's own inventory at GUI Scale 3, and
at Largest (or GUI Scale Auto) — as at GUI Scale 4.

1752.content:
A switch under Mod window size, **off** by default. Off, the storage terminal opens with its search box unfocused, so the
inventory key (E) closes it like any container; to search, click the box or press / or Tab (Ctrl+F works too). On, letters go
straight into the search as soon as the terminal opens, but E then types into the search instead of closing the window (Esc
clears the search first, then closes). The setting is yours alone: it is stored on your computer, not on the server.

1753.content:
The mod plays the game's own recordings: each action has its own set, pitch and rhythm, and every ship has its own takeoff,
landing and maneuver sounds. The synthesized "Own sounds" are gone from the mod. Working machines hum (the four nearest within
sixteen blocks are heard), a ship's afterburner has a roar of its own, and a lair guardian waking or a gate crossing is marked
by a sound.

1754.content: The mod settings have two switches above the Done button, both on by default:

1755.content: **Aircraft sounds**: the ships' own takeoff, landing and maneuver sounds; off, a ship plays the older shared recordings;

1756.content: **Ambience sounds**: the sound backdrop of the worlds (below); off, it falls silent at once.

1757.content:
With the game's subtitles on, the mod's actions carry captions of their own: "The Blind Spot clot draws breath",
"The Wayfarer passes a corridor gate", "The light is whole again": one line per action, not the names of the recordings
it is built from.

1758.content:
Every world of the mod has its own soundscape — not music, but the place itself. For example, the muffled steady wind of Mars (darker and
slower at night) and the rolling steam of the Breath. Each biome adds its own layer: an airy drone with a distant shimmer on the
Martian Plains, a warm breathing tone in the Martian Dunes, a deep stone drone in the Martian Canyons, cold wind over ice on the
Martian Polar Cap, and the warm hum of charged air in the Vapors of the Breath. Now and then something short sounds nearby —
pebbles, a whirl of wind, cracking ice or a rockfall on Mars; thunder, sizzling acid and clinking glass on the Breath — and caves
have their own rumble. Every few seconds a quiet phrase of two to four notes plays on different steps of a scale (a mallet on Mars,
a chime on the Breath).

1759.content:
The ambience sits under the game's own sounds: footsteps, mobs and your voice chat stay on top. Its volume is the game's
"Ambient/Environment" slider; under a roof and in caves the background is quieter, and so it is during world weather (weather has
its own sounds). On low Mod graphics the notes play less often and the phrases are shorter. The mod setting Ambience sounds turns it off.

1760.content:
The mod’s hints, alarms and messages never cover each other: every line has its own place, and when it gets crowded the
less important one gives way.

1761.content:
**Top center** — boss bars, their phase hints and event banners, then the jump progress, the autopilot, anomaly alarms
and the mod line while in a ship.

1762.content:
**Below the crosshair** — central alarms (“no fuel for take-off”, a comet jet) and the ore scanner summary; the more
important one stays closer to the crosshair.

1763.content:
**Above the hotbar** — the mod line; it steps around recent chat messages and the suit bars, and fades over the chat while
you are typing.

1764.content:
**Corners** — the comms header (ship, deck, big moments) top left, the target and effect icons top right, coordinates
bottom right. The task card yields its corner to the comms header.

1765.content:
When there is not enough room, a less important line first gets shorter (a single line) and then folds into “+N” at the
end of its column — and comes back as soon as there is room again.

1766.content:
The mod's windows follow the game's GUI Scale setting, like the game's own screens: Auto looks as before, and a smaller scale
makes a window smaller and gives it more room (on 1920×1080 and larger screens); to make them larger at the same scale, use
Mod window size. The mod's HUD stays as it is.

1779.content: The whole mod starts with the sky. The journal tells you what to do next, and the telescope opens the first worlds.

is the book that guides you through the mod: chapters are branches of the path, stages are
goals. Every stage has a “what to do” hint. The journal is made from a book and lapis lazuli:

1781.content:
On your first visit the journal is already in your hand. When you complete a stage, a line above the hotbar says so and
names the next one.

1782.content:
The first time you open it, the journal asks about the **mod graphics** — low, medium or high. You can change it later in
the settings (the gear in the journal’s header).

1783.content:
Stages with a structure made of several blocks (the larger telescopes, rockets, the radio telescope, the emitter, the
shipyard, the gate ring) have a **scheme** in the journal: you can turn it and view it layer by layer. The **“Show in the
world”** button places a ghost of the structure on the ground a few steps in front of you (or on the block you are looking
at, if it is close) — it appears from the bottom up, with a column of light above the spot. Only you see the ghost. Build
over it from the bottom up: the lowest unfinished layer is brighter, the heart is golden, and blocks with something in the
way are red. If you were looking at the sky or at your feet, a line above the hotbar tells you which side the ghost is on
and how far. The same button in the journal removes it; a finished structure removes the ghost by itself.

1784.content: The journal shows every recipe of an item: the one earlier on the path comes first, and the arrows beside it switch to the rest.

1785.content:
Joined a friend on a server who has gone far ahead, or the other way round? A  carries knowledge
from one journal to another. Blank copies are crafted from a book and quill, a glow ink sac and stardust:

1786.content:
**Fill it**: hold a blank copy with your Star Journal in the other hand and right-click. It costs 8 stardust. Pages fly from
the journal into the copy; the copy's tooltip says whose records they are and how many stages and finds they hold. Your own
filled copy can be filled again with fresh records.

1787.content:
**Write it in**: the friend takes the filled copy and right-clicks; no journal needed in hand. Everything is written in at once,
quietly, with no stage rewards; what the reader already had stays. A stage page that came this way says "Copied from the
journal of …" instead of "Completed". The copy is blank again afterwards.

1788.content:
**What it carries is knowledge**: journal stages, found constellations, worlds, rifts and vents (so the friend can travel
there), the Atlas of Life, spectra, ship blueprints, navigation records and the understood signs of
the gate script.

1789.content:
**What stays personal is deeds**: first landings, victories over masters and guardians, events lived through, tablets read
and their rewards, your own rockets, ships, station and beacons, the trust and tasks of the peoples.

1790.content:
Your own copy does nothing for you ("give the copy to a friend"), a copy of a copy cannot be made, and a copy is written in
only once. A world remembers up to eight unread copies per author: the ninth fades the oldest one.

8142.content: Where the haze is thickest, tholins clump together into amber and the amber keeps growing: stalks, globes and caps on a patch of peach cloud

8144.content: An ice giant lying on its side: it rolls along its orbit like a ball.

8146.content: A jet of methane that burst out of the cloud and froze before it could fall.

8148.content: A storehouse for things that had to stay cold, built where nothing ever thaws.

8150.content: A cone of methane ice boulders stacked one on another, with a column of three hailstones on top.

8152.content: An expedition came to Uranus for diamonds: here they fall from the sky as hail.

8154.content: A survey probe that froze in flight.

8156.content: The same ring as on Earth, on a dais of the local stone and in the colors of this world: whoever set the gates out did it on every world at

8158.content: A platform on legs above the cloud, with three habitat modules around a hub and a mast that still carries a light.

8160.content: Two pressure ridges of methane ice with an arch of packed ice sprung between them.

8162.content: An observatory tower that fell on its side and lies where it fell, dome and all.

8166.content: An expedition came to Neptune for black diamonds: deep down, the pressure squeezes carbon into stones, and they fall as rain.

8168.content: A twisted spire of indigo cloud grown through with diamond, leaning the way the wind blows.

8170.content: Eight stelae of cobalt cloud around a slab of black stone, each with an eye of black diamond on top.

8172.content: The same ring as on Earth, on a dais of the local stone and in the colors of this world: whoever set the gates out did it on every world at

8174.content: A probe kite that was flown into the wind to measure it.

8176.content: An anchor of station trim standing on its flukes in the cloud, with a chain that goes up twelve links, leans east with the wind and ends in

8178.content: A habitat module that was set down on the cloud and has been going under ever since: the windows are at cloud level, the east side is alread

8180.content: A sphere of white cloud and superionic ice, sunk to its waist in the cloud.

8182.content: A mast, a slanted neck and seven chains strung between them across the wind, each shorter than the last.

8186.content: Ceres is not quite dead: here the brine still finds its way up.

8188.content: The camp of the Dawn expedition.

8190.content: Three mirrors under the salt of Occator, older than the salt itself.

8192.content: A shell of ice thirty blocks thick over a sea sixty deep.

8194.content: A hut with a beacon on the ice, a shaft through the whole shell, and a glass sphere hanging under it in the dark sea.

8196.content: A dark hull eighty blocks long on the floor of the ocean, ribbed with rings taller than any ship of yours.

8198.content: The most volcanic body in the Solar System: Jupiter kneads Io with its tides, and the heat comes out through four hundred volcanoes.

8200.content: Io and Jupiter are joined by a current of three million amperes; where it comes down, somebody drove masts into the ground.

8202.content: A bell taller than a house hangs over an island in the lava lake of Loki, and nobody on Io could have cast it.

8204.content: A dome of watchers by a volcano that has not gone out since the Voyagers saw it in 1979.

8206.content: The only moon with an atmosphere, and the only world besides Earth with seas — but the seas are liquid methane, and the rock is water ice.

8208.content: A rotorcraft the size of a car: on Titan the air is so dense and the gravity so weak that flying is easier than walking.

8210.content: Huygens came down here on a parachute on January 14, 2005, and talked for seventy-two minutes from the surface: the farthest landing ever ma

8212.content: A tower on an island in the Kraken Sea.

8214.content: The whitest world in the Solar System: its snow falls from its own geysers.

8216.content: A jet that the cold caught in flight: arcs of blue ice over a mound of snow, each ending in icicles.

8218.content: A station that sieved the snow of the jets: the funnel on the mast caught what fell, the crates below took it.

8220.content: Four dark pipes over the warm heart of the tiger stripes, set by someone long before the snow.

8222.content: A world sewn from patches: plates half a thousand blocks across, each at its own height and tilt, dark seams between them.

8224.content: A court at the point of the bright chevron, cut across by a dark seam.

8226.content: Where two patches of Miranda meet, the dark ice has grown crystals as tall as a house — twins joined at an angle, every pair a chevron.

8228.content: A beacon on the brink of Verona Rupes, the highest cliff anyone knows.

8230.content: A captured world: Triton runs around Neptune backwards.

8232.content: Nine links of dark iron, each as tall as a tower, rise out of the pink ice — and go on into the sky as light, toward Neptune.

8234.content: A mound of dark dust around a nitrogen geyser.

8236.content: A mooring of those who came down the chain from Neptune: a deck on piles, two masts, an anchor post of the same dark iron.

8252.content: A tall smithy of crystal brick with a chimney higher than its roof, floored in plating that came through the rift with the smiths.

8258.content: A round shaft six blocks deep with a stair winding down its wall.

8260.content: A long hall of crystal brick with mirrors of dark glass between its pilasters and a greater mirror at the far end, framed in light.

8262.content: Two pillars of prism glass on a paved dais, with a stepped lintel between them and nothing in the opening.

8273.content: A ring of fused glass and lightning-glass on an island shard, with three eggs in the bowl.

8275.content: A shuttle dock of station flooring laid on the vapor, with its diving hut and its tether reel.

8277.content: Every bolt that strikes an island leaves a column of fused glass standing where it went in.

8279.content: The Ringers came to the Breath for its lightning.

8281.content: The same ring as on Earth, on a dais of the local stone and in the colors of this world: whoever set the gates out did it on every world at

8287.content: A brick tower on an island shard, with a lantern in its crown and a rod above it.

8289.content: A frame of fulgurite with five chimes hanging from it on chains: three bells and two bars of searing glass.

8291.content: Hexagonal combs of purpur stacked into columns and wells full of chorus wax.

8293.content: A spire of comb wall that leans a little to the east, shot through with amber that grows thicker toward the crown.

8295.content: A span of purpur slab and brick rail between two comb pillars, raised a little toward the middle.

8297.content: A single pillar of comb wall with branches of slab reaching out at three heights, each ending in a small platform cupped with wax.

8301.content: A pointed arch of purpur brick standing on its own, with cells cut into both piers and a threshold worn smooth.

8303.content: A six-sided chamber of purpur brick, taller than any other cell, with a cocoon of wax and amber hanging under its roof.

8305.content: A lumpy dome of comb cap with an eye at the top and a torn way in at the side.

8307.content: A six-sided hall of comb wall with a floor of poured wax and cells in every wall, some sealed, some empty.

8312.content: A six-sided shaft lined with brick, seven blocks deep, with a ledge winding down its wall.

8314.content: A world that is an eye: a black pupil pit in the middle and an iris of fibers in rings around it — a golden rim and golden rays by the pupil

8316.content: Two leaves of sclera brick on either side of a gap three blocks wide, with a plate of pupil glass for a threshold.

8318.content: The same ring as on Earth, on a dais of the local stone and in the colors of this world: whoever set the gates out did it on every world at

8322.content: Seven curved pillars of sclera stone along a ridge at the edge of the Eye, every one leaning away from the pupil.

8324.content: A leaning crystal taller than a house, driven into the iris point first and standing on its own weight, with the ground torn up around it.

8326.content: A stepped pit dug into the groove of the iris for pigment nodules: the color of the Eye, ground into the coatings of lenses.

8328.content: A pier of void plating on piles over the black glass of the pupil: the only solid footing there is.

8332.content: Vessels of the white rise out of the ground here, loop over one another in a knot the size of a house and go back under.

8334.content: A hollow in the iris walled with woven fiber and spiked with gaze crystal.

8359.content: A pier of scorched plating on heat piers, running out over the golden sea from a slag shore.

8365.content: A desert of soul ash under ribs of giants, lit by soul fire that gives no warmth.

8367.content: A brick well with a bone windlass over it and a chain going down into the dark.

8369.content: Two giant bones set upright on brick plinths with a rib arched between them, and a paved road running through the gap.

8374.content: Stumps of soul cinder standing on a patch of baked ground, blue fire on every third one.

8376.content: Three sledges on heatproof runners, chained one behind the other and sunk to the runners in soul ash.

8382.content: A chewed-through piece of giant bone lying in the ash, and under it a hole going down.

8384.content: A paved ring with a crib of giant bone in the middle and blue fire inside the crib.

8386.content: A long barrow of packed ash with curb stones round it and a dolmen at the east end.

8390.content: Three felt domes grown together, waist-deep in the ground, with a crawlway in from the south.

8396.content: A cluster of thin bent stalks from one felt cushion, each hung with a bell that is lit from inside.

8398.content: The stump of a titan that lost its cap long ago, with bracket fungi climbing it in a spiral, each one a step above the last.

8400.content: A fruiting body taller than a titan is wide, ribbed like a pipe organ, with a spiral of lit pits up its side.

8402.content: The first bell that came down the vent never went back up.

8405.content: A weaving shed of scorched plating on heat piers, and under it a loom strung with glowing thread.

8407.content: A mushroom taller than a tower, red cap and white warts, with gills of glowing thread underneath that light the ground for twenty paces.

8409.content: The largest thing that grows here, and the palest: a white cap wider than a house on a stalk you could hollow a room into, and someone has.

8411.content: An old titan of the warped growth: the cap has flattened and turned up at the edge like a dish, so the glowing gills show all the way round.

8413.content: The skeleton of something longer than a bell is tall, with bones of copper gone green to the marrow.
